## Goal

Notebook 10 of case study 2 made the network reconstruction (`miic()`) about 3 times faster with three patches of
`miic`, tested on the humanSkin data. Here we check the patched version on another dataset, the authors' job of case
study 1 on the official CausalCCC web server (miic.curie.fr, job `eaP9Br0llvzxN07zZZEC`, 21 January 2025), and compare
its running time with the server's.

Two versions of `miic` are compared:

- **Stock miic** (variant `baseline`): the `miic` package used by CausalCCC (branch `causalccc`, commit `5ca0b22`),
  compiled as is, without any change of ours. It is the code the server runs.
- **Patched miic** (variant `deterministic`): the same code with three patches (`envs/patches/miic/`):
  1. **no console message from worker threads**: stock `miic` prints messages (`Rcout`) from its OpenMP threads, which
     makes it crash with more than one thread on case study 2. This is what makes 8 threads usable;
  2. **early decision of the confidence cut**: the 100 shuffles of a link stop as soon as keeping or removing it is
     certain, so the exported `confidence` of those links becomes a bound, while decisions stay the same;
  3. **exact ties broken by position**: when two candidates have exactly the same score, the choice no longer depends
     on the order in which threads finish.

Each local run is compared with the server's network (links, orientations, genuine causations, values) and timed.
The runs are made outside this notebook, one after another on an idle machine (WSL Ubuntu 24.04, R 4.6.1, 12 cores,
7.8 GB of memory), with the server's settings (`scripts/run_miic.R`):

```bash
bash scripts/case1/download_case1.sh                   # only the server job files are needed here
bash scripts/benchmarks/build_miic_variant.sh baseline  # and deterministic, see notebook 10 of case study 2
bash scripts/benchmarks/run_case1_benchmarks.sh         # 7 runs, about 1 hour
Rscript scripts/benchmarks/compare_case1.R              # writes results/benchmarks/case1_server_vs_local.tsv
```

**Inputs:** the authors' server job in `data/case1/causalccc_server_eaP9Br0llvzxN07zZZEC/` (read only) and the runs in
`results/benchmarks/miic/case1/`. **Output:** `results/benchmarks/case1_server_vs_local.tsv`.

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)

root <- getwd()
while (!file.exists(file.path(root, "scripts", "helpers.R"))) {
  if (dirname(root) == root) stop("Repository root not found. Open the repository folder in Positron.")
  root <- dirname(root)
}
source(file.path(root, "scripts", "helpers.R"))
source(file.path(root, "scripts", "benchmarks", "compare_outputs.R"))

job_dir   <- file.path(root, "data", "case1", "causalccc_server_eaP9Br0llvzxN07zZZEC")
bench_dir <- file.path(root, "results", "benchmarks", "miic", "case1")
if (!dir.exists(job_dir)) stop("Data not found: run scripts/case1/download_case1.sh first.")
```

## 1. Same input?

The local runs read the server's own input files, so only identical columns could still cause trouble (they made
multithreaded orientations unstable on case study 2, notebook 10). The mosaic has none:

```{r}
#| label: duplicates

mosaic      <- read_tsv(file.path(job_dir, "input.tsv"), guess_max = Inf, show_col_types = FALSE)
state_order <- read_tsv(file.path(job_dir, "clean_state_order.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

group    <- set_names(state_order$group, state_order$var_names)[names(mosaic)]
col_type <- if_else(group %in% c("ligands", "senders genes"), "senders", "receivers")
row_type <- if_else(!is.na(mosaic[[which(col_type == "senders")[1]]]), "senders", "receivers")
tibble(cells = nrow(mosaic), variables = ncol(mosaic),
       duplicated_columns = length(duplicated_columns(mosaic, row_type, col_type)))
```

## 2. Server network against local runs

The server's network is `edgesList.miic.summary.txt_save`, the file written by the run itself (the April 2025 edit of
`edgesList.miic.summary.txt` only changes the values of the 18 L-R links, `data/README.md`). Each local run is
compared with it and with the stock one-thread run (`compare_miic()`, `scripts/benchmarks/compare_outputs.R`).

```{r}
#| label: comparisons

server <- list(all.edges.summary = read_tsv(file.path(job_dir, "edgesList.miic.summary.txt_save"),
                                            show_col_types = FALSE))
runs <- c("baseline_t1", "baseline_t2", paste0("deterministic_t", c(1, 2, 4, 8, 12)))
results <- set_names(map(file.path(bench_dir, runs, "miic_result.rds"), readRDS), runs)

comparisons <- map_dfr(runs, \(r) bind_rows(
  server   = compare_miic(server, results[[r]]),
  stock_t1 = compare_miic(results$baseline_t1, results[[r]]), .id = "against") |>
    mutate(run = r, .before = 1))
comparisons |>
  select(run, against, verdict, links_new, orientations_changed, causal_changed,
         max_diff_info_shifted, max_diff_confidence, links_confidence_diff) |>
  mutate(max_diff_info_shifted = signif(max_diff_info_shifted, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## 3. Running times

The server's time is the one `miic` prints at the end of its search in `whole_run.log` ("TIME : 935"); the local times
are those `miic` records (`$time`), with the wall clock and peak memory from GNU `time`.

```{r}
#| label: summary

summary <- read_tsv(file.path(root, "results", "benchmarks", "case1_server_vs_local.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
summary |>
  transmute(setup, miic, threads,
            miic_time = sprintf("%.0f s (%.1f min)", miic_s, miic_s / 60),
            peak_mb = round(peak_mb), links, verdict_vs_server,
            speedup_vs_server = sprintf("x%.2f", speedup_vs_server),
            speedup_vs_stock_t1 = sprintf("x%.2f", speedup_vs_stock_t1)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## What we learned

**The patched miic gives the server's network.** Every local run, stock or patched, on 1, 2 or 8 threads, has the
server's 364 retained links, its orientations and its 13 genuine causations. Link strengths (`info_shifted`) differ by
less than 10⁻¹³ (rounding). The verdict "same decisions, values differ" is the best possible against the server: its
file stores values rounded to 6 decimals and its random seed is not ours.

**Only `confidence` moves, and never enough to change a decision.** With stock miic it differs from the server's by
up to 0.0009 on 10 links (another random seed for the shuffles). With the patched miic, by up to 0.009 on 132 links,
already on one thread: this is change 2, which stops the shuffles of a link once its decision is certain, so its
`confidence` is a bound rather than the full estimate.

**What "stock" and "patched" mean.** Stock miic is the `miic` package of CausalCCC (branch `causalccc`) compiled as is:
the code the server runs. The patched miic (`deterministic`) is the same code with three changes: no console message
from worker threads (stock miic crashes with several threads on case study 2), early decision of the confidence cut, and
exact ties broken by position (results independent of thread timing). Comparing them at the same number of threads
isolates the effect of the patches.

**The patches do not make miic faster by themselves; they make 8 threads usable and reliable.** At equal threads the
patched version is as fast as stock (1 thread: 834 vs 825 s; 2 threads: 486 vs 457 s). The gain comes from using 8
threads: 288 s (4.8 min), 2.9 times faster than stock on one thread and 3.3 times faster than the server (935 s,
15.6 min, 2 threads), as on case study 2 (÷ 3). The server's hardware is not ours: on the same settings this laptop is
already 1.13 times faster on one thread than the server on two, so only the local comparisons measure the code.

**More threads help less and less; 12 is the maximum of this laptop.** Patched miic takes 834 s on 1 thread, 486 s on
2, 371 s on 4, 288 s on 8 and 262 s on 12 (÷ 3.2 against one thread, ÷ 3.6 against the server), always with the
server's decisions. The i7-1365U has 10 cores (2 performance cores with hyper-threading, 8 efficiency cores without),
i.e. 12 logical CPUs, already counted by `nproc`: more than 12 threads would only share them. Going from 8 to 12 threads
saves 26 s (9 %) because the 4 extra threads are hyper-threads and slower efficiency cores, and because the main loop of
`iter` treats one link at a time (notebook 10 of case study 2). 8 threads leave the machine usable for a 9 % cost;
12 threads are worth it for unattended runs.

**Stock miic did not crash on 2 threads here**, unlike case study 2 with 4 threads; it was not tried on 8 threads, and
case study 1 has no duplicated columns, so the tie-breaking of change 3 was not put to the test. For larger datasets
(thymus) the patched variant on 8 threads remains the safe choice.
